FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Explain the difference between a diagnosis based on pathophysiology and a diagnosis based
on symptoms and signs alone.
List the potential disadvantages and advantages of diagnoses that suggest pathophysiology
that cannot be verified objectively.
Identify diagnostic debates and treatment challenges associated with nonspecific painful
illness, such as fibromyalgia, radial tunnel syndrome, and type 1 complex regional pain
syndrome.
Overview
Some patients present with pain and no measurable pathophysiology.

A number of constructs of unclear benefit are suggested for nonspecific pain, including
fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), and central
sensitization.
Some debated nonspecific pain diagnoses are constructed as a rationale for surgical
management, including radial tunnel syndrome, pronator syndrome, and others. These merit
special attention given the inherent potential for harm with surgical management.
Epidemiology
Nonspecific symptoms are common. As many as 50% of all symptoms brought to medical
attention are never linked to a specific pathology.1-3
The prevalence of unexplained daily pain as an illness (brought to the continued attention of
clinicians) is estimated to be less than 1%.4-7

Epidemiology
One vexing problem in health care is pain without a clearly associated pathophysiology.
Estimates of prevalence encompass a large range and are inherently difficult to measure
because of lack of clarity in diagnosis.
Numerous conceptual frameworks or constructs have been suggested to describe
nonspecific pain, including fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, CRPS, and central
sensitization. Because these are not experimentally verifiable, they represent social
constructions (entities that exist because society agrees they exist). Some socially
constructed illnesses, such as radial tunnel syndrome and pronator syndrome, are used
as a rationale for surgical management. Socially constructed illnesses that lead to
surgical management merit special attention. Because of the inherent and potential
harms of surgical management, ethics require that surgical management of speculative
pathophysiology be held to a standard of needing to demonstrate a potential benefit
beyond nonspecific effects, including the placebo effect. These diagnoses are used
variably, and surgeons should be aware of the ethical dilemmas and debates
surrounding them.

Definition
A hallmark of nonspecific pain conditions is the absence of objectively measurable
pathophysiology.
A diagnostic label may misleadingly suggest objective pathology exists in a patient in whom the
construct is speculative.
The potential advantages and disadvantages of the application of specific diagnostic labels to
nonspecific painful illnesses merit careful consideration.
On initial presentation and subsequent evaluation, surgeons must consider discrete, verifiable,
manageable pathophysiology. A diagnosis of nonspecific pain is based on repeat patient
history and physical examination.
Definition

Definition
Fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue, and central sensitization are diagnostic constructs applied
to patients who have unexplained pain. A common thread in these diagnoses is the
absence of objectively measurable pathophysiology.5 In some constructs, a diagnosis is
offered only in the absence of any other discrete, verifiable pathophysiology. Radial
tunnel syndrome is characterized by pain, no atrophy or sensory abnormalities, and
normal electrodiagnostic testing. This is compared with posterior interosseous nerve
syndrome, which is defined by motor palsy and abnormal electrodiagnostic studies. Type
2 CRPS is a label applied to disproportionate symptoms and incapability in the presence
of discrete neuropathology. Conversely, type 1 CRPS is defined by the absence of
discrete, objectively measurable pathophysiology. Surgeons must understand that this is
an approach based on the concept that a diagnostic label is beneficial for nonspecific
symptoms, which is a subject of debate and is distinct from diagnosis based on
objectively measurable pathophysiology.
Surgeons must consider the estimated prevalence of patients with nonspecific pain seen
once or a few times by a clinician (very common), daily nonspecific pain as an illness
(ongoing medical attention; much less common, suggesting most symptoms resolve or
are accommodated), and the prevalence of patients who likely have a discrete diagnosis.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:51 PM
AAOS | Nonspecific Pain
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000512
3/16

Knowledge of these base rates is important to avoid the base rate fallacy, in which the
likelihood of the problem is overestimated or underestimated because the relative
prevalence of various possibilities is not adequately weighted. Nonspecific pain
constructs merit thoughtful and limited use given that, in a usual practice, the
prevalence of nonspecific pain conditions is common at initial evaluation and less than
1% among the population, which is relatively uncommon compared with conditions with
a clear pathophysiology.
A patient labeled with an illness construct may face a stigma that creates an obstacle to
subsequent treatment. Such a label may make clinicians less curious about the potential
pathophysiology. Conversely, such a label may reinforce a reluctance to discuss the
cognitive and emotional aspects of illness in that mental health considerations are
offensive or inappropriate.8 Surgeons must recognize this complex situation and
maintain an awareness of these barriers during care of these patients. Patients like to
have a name for their condition; however, the application of these diagnostic constructs
may have unanticipated repercussions.
Surgeons should consider the following factors in approaching patients presenting for
treatment of troubling unexplained pain:
It may be useful to have a colleague see the patient to ensure that no manageable pathology
is overlooked. Consensus that a problem is nonspecific may be useful for the clinician and
the patient.
If a specific diagnosis is being considered for a nonspecific illness, surgeons should consider
the potential disadvantages and consult a colleague who has a different mindset. Often, this
can be done via a case presentation or via a post to a professional group for the input of
colleagues and does not always need to be a formal consultation. Each patient deserves
access to a diverse set of opinions on nonspecific pain as much as that for a specific
pathology.
For patients labeled with a specific diagnostic construct by another clinician, surgeons must
confirm that an alternative diagnosis has not been overlooked. Surgeons should be aware of
anchoring bias and use appropriate de-biasing strategies in consideration of the symptoms.

Be judicious with diagnostic testing, especially repeat testing. Only order tests intended to
confirm a diagnosis for which the pre-test odds are reasonably high based on the patient
history and physical examination findings. In a patient in whom a diagnosis is unlikely, a
diagnostic test is much more likely to yield a false-positive result. Even a test with a high
sensitivity and specificity will be problematic. For example, if a test is 99% specific and 99%
sensitive for the diagnosis of Ebola and 100,000 people in a city without Ebola are tested,
1,000 people will have a false-positive result.
Remember that monitoring over time is a very useful clinical approach. This approach helps
balance the potential to overlook important pathology against the potential for iatrogenic
harm via over-testing and overtreating.
Providing care over time also helps build a trusting relationship that can help unearth
important symptoms, such as despair, worry, and common misconceptions. A strong
relationship can help with the gentle reorientation of these misconceptions.
Anticipate pressure from patients to find the problem promptly, and prepare effective
communication strategies.
Remain humble, curious, and collaborative. Although a specific, objectively measurable
pathology that will one day be discovered is unlikely, the patient and the specialist can
remain open to this possibility.
Another manner of stating this is that part of good health is acceptance of some degree of
uncertainty and overlooked pathology.
Psychosocial Contributors
Notable symptoms of depression are a common comorbidity in patients seeking treatment for
troubling, persistent pain.
The prevalence of comorbid depression ranges from 64% to 75% in patients seeking treatment
for persistent pain.9,10
Cognitive behavioral therapy and mindfulness-based treatment option may aid in reducing
pain intensity and symptoms of psychological distress.


Psychosocial Contributors
Comorbid clinical depression and generalized anxiety disorder is reported in 20% to 80%
and 13% to 64% of patients with fibromyalgia, respectively. The reasons for these wide
ranges are unclear.
The recognition that symptoms of depression and anxiety are associated with greater
pain intensity in various contexts has drastically changed perspectives in orthopaedics
over the past decade, and a deeper understanding of the interplay of these factors has
been achieved.
Types of psychological treatment options include cognitive behavioral therapy and
mindfulness interventions.11,12 Cognitive behavioral therapy is based on the principle
that mental health is partially caused by unhelpful patterns of thinking and behavior;
recognition of these pattens and conscious attempts to cultivate more healthy thoughts
are beneficial. Mindfulness seeks to build on the principles of cognitive-based therapy by
focusing on paying attention to thoughts without passing judgment on them. These
interventions are effective in reducing pain and psychologic distress and are increasingly
being used in the care of orthopaedic patients with chronic pain of clear or unclear
etiology.
Fibromyalgia
Diagnostic criteria continue to evolve and remain subjective. Current criteria include the
following:
Nonspecific pain and symptoms in multiple areas of the body
Symptoms lasting at least 3 months
No other health problem that explains the pain and symptoms

Fibromyalgia
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:51 PM
AAOS | Nonspecific Pain
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000512
6/16

Fibromyalgia was historically diagnosed by the presence of multiple painful sites for
more than 3 months without an alternative diagnosis.13-16 These criteria were revised in
2010 by the American College of Rheumatology and are less dependent on a tenderness
test. Currently, fibromyalgia is characterized by chronic pain in four of five regions: axial,
left upper limb, right upper limb, left lower limb, and right lower limb.
The name and diagnostic criteria of socially constructed diagnoses typically evolve over
time. Identification of an underlying pathology for nonspecific diagnoses over time is
uncommon. An example of eventually identifying a pathology is a peptic ulcer that was
thought to be stress-related eventually is determined to be the result of infection via
Helicobacter pylori.
The diagnosis of fibromyalgia may have a gender bias. In applying current criteria to
patients who were diagnosed via older criteria, Wolfe et al16 found that women may be
over-diagnosed.
Treatment options for fibromyalgia include exercise and counseling. Some
pharmacologic options include NSAIDs and antidepressant medications. Antidepressant
medications are offered while the potential mental health contributions to the illness are
not always discussed. In addition, the role of cognitive behavioral therapy may be
underrecognized or under-recommended but may be helpful.
Radial Tunnel Syndrome
Radial tunnel syndrome is characterized as lateral arm pain without motor or sensory changes
on physical examination or detectable neurophysiologic abnormalities.
Case series document palliation of symptoms with surgical management; however, complexity
in establishing a diagnosis and the potential for improvements unrelated to alterations in
pathophysiology via nonspecific effects, creates challenges for interpreting these uncontrolled
series.

Radial Tunnel Syndrome
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:51 PM
AAOS | Nonspecific Pain
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000512
7/16

Radial tunnel syndrome is thought to arise from compression of the radial nerve to a
degree that leads to compression of pain fibers but does not result in sensory or motor
changes.17,18 This clinical entity is highly debated among surgeons because this nerve
condition is unmeasurable. Electrodiagnostic studies are normal.
The presentation is characterized as a deep ache in the lateral elbow, distal to the lateral
epicondyle. Differential diagnoses include lateral epicondylosis and radiocapitellar
arthrosis. Specific physical examination maneuvers intended to distinguish radial tunnel
syndrome from these other diagnoses include pain with resisted supination and pain
with long finger extension; however, the reliability and accuracy of these tests is difficult
to verify experimentally, and these physical examination maneuvers may result in pain in
patients with lateral epicondylosis.
Numerous case series demonstrate clinical improvement after surgical release of the
radial nerve.19-22 The results of many of these studies are substantial and warrant
serious consideration. Surgeons also should consider studies comparing the subjective
outcomes of simulated knee arthroscopy for the management of degenerative meniscal
pathology with those of subacromial decompression for the management of rotator cuff
tendinopathy, which have not shown any benefit. The ideal study would randomize
patients to simulated versus actual radial tunnel release, with blinding of everyone and
the patient contacted after the procedure. Until such a study is performed, uncertainty
and debate regarding this clinical entity will exist.
Five sites of compression are commonly described in radial tunnel syndrome:
Fibrous bands anterior to the radiocapitellar joint
Radial recurrent vessels
Medial edge of the extensor carpi radialis brevis
Arcade of Frohse—the proximal tendinous edge of the supinator
Distal edge of the superficial head of the supinator

Type 1 CRPS
CRPS is divided into two types.
In type 1, no clear etiology for the pain exists
In type 2, the syndrome is related to an identifiable nerve injury or compression
CRPS 1 is heterogeneous in presentation and variably diagnosed.
A common set of criteria offer a diagnosis of type 1 CRPS if three of four criteria are met.
Disproportionate pain
Symptoms
Signs
No other explanation
These criteria are never satisfied because another explanation always is possible.8 For
example, injury and overprotection likely are the explanation for most patients with criteria
one through three.23-25 Catastrophic thinking generally is the source of findings one through
three, which is a better explanation, making type 1 CRPS unhelpful and potentially distracting
from the manageable misinterpretation of symptoms.
Signs and symptoms are categorized in four areas.
Sensory
Vasomotor
Sudomotor/edema
Motor/trophic
The role of imaging studies, such as three-phase bone scintigraphy, in diagnosis is
controversial.26
Radiographs may demonstrate findings suggestive of disuse osteopenia, which is not sensitive
or specific.

Type 1 CRPS
CRPS is a condition characterized by a heterogeneous presentation of disproportionate
pain and incapability with varying sensory, vascular, and trophic changes.27,28 Several
guidelines are used to diagnose CRPS. The most common is the Budapest Criteria, which
offer a diagnosis of CRPS if three of four criteria are met (Table 1). In addition, two types
of CRPS exist. Type 1 has no discrete etiology, whereas type 2 is associated with an
identifiable nerve injury (Figures 1 and 2).

Limited interobserver reliability for individual criteria exists, and diagnostic agreement
between different criteria is poor. Some surgeons have suggested using three-phase
bone scintigraphy for diagnosis; however, diagnosis is made if tracer activity is increased
or decreased in bone. Concordance between three-phase bone scans and diagnostic
criteria varies widely, and the use of bone scintigraphy is a subject of debate.
Figure 1 Clinical photograph of bilateral hands shows complex regional pain syndrome
of the left hand, with hypertrichosis, oedema, joint stiffness, nail changes, and skin
atrophy. Some mirror image changes are observed in the right hand. (Reproduced with
permission from WikiMSK: CRPS. Available at: https://wikimsk.org/wiki/CRPS. Accessed
November 4, 2022.)
Some surgeons describe three stages of CRPS. In stage 1 (acute), pain is accompanied by
changes in skin color and temperature; in stage 2 (subacute), worsening pain is
accompanied by joint stiffness. In stage 3 (chronic), somewhat diminished pain is
associated with joint contracture and severe osteopenia.

be accounted for by psychological distress, psychopathology, and ineffective coping
strategies. Surgeons must recognize these contributions and incorporate cognitive
behavioral therapy into the treatment approach.
